title: News Words: Embers
description:
Welcome to the Voice of America’s News Words.                 

In January, sudden wildfires caused massive destruction in and around Los Angeles, California. 
                                         
EMBERS  

The Palisades and Eaton wildfires caused 29 deaths and the destruction of more than 16,000 structures including homes, schools and shops. The causes of the fires are under investigation but officials say it is possible that strong winds fueled embers from an earlier fire. 

Embers are small pieces of burning coal or wood from a fire. 
In some cases, embers are as hot as the fire that created them.

title: News Words: Immense
description:
Welcome to the Voice of America’s News Words.                 

A ceasefire between Israel and Hamas took effect in mid-January.
                           
IMMENSE             

Part one of the ceasefire is 42 days long. It suspends a war that began in 2023 after Hamas attacked Israel and Israel responded in Hamas-led Gaza. After the ceasefire, displaced Gazans returned to their homes to find immense destruction.     
              
Immense describes something very large in size or amount.
An ocean can be described as an immense body of water. 
A similar adjective is huge.

title: Elephants in court, Missing school, Changing workplace for science, Hafta
description:
Podcast for Wednesday, Jan 29 

On today’s podcast, Caty Weaver and Mario Ritter, Jr. host the show. Caty tells listeners what they are going to hear.
(1:14) First, Caty has a story about an unusual legal case in the American West. The Supreme Court of the western state of Colorado recently ruled that elephants in a zoo could not seek release from a zoo because they are not human. An animal rights group argued the elephants should be placed in a special sanctuary. https://learningenglish.voanews.com/a/colorado-court-rules-elephants-barred-from-seeking-zoo-release-are-not-humans/7948893.html 
(5:49) Then, Bryan Lynn reports on a recent study that finds bad weather is keeping children around the world from school. A United Nations report has found that extreme weather interrupted schooling for at least 242 million children in 2024. These weather events included heatwaves, storms, dry conditions, and flooding. Countries in Asia and Africa were most affected, but every area reported school children missing class including in Europe where heavy flooding was reported. Heat waves also caused a lot of missed class. https://learningenglish.voanews.com/a/un-says-250-million-students-missed-school-in-2024-because-of-weather/7951724.html 
(11:00) After that, Caty and Mario present Education Tips. This week, they have a story about disabled college teachers and students. Researchers with disabilities often face barriers that others do not. A recent outing in Southern California gave a group of disabled researchers a chance to discuss how they face their problems and aim for good results. https://learningenglish.voanews.com/a/scientists-with-disabilities-seek-changes-to-improve-their-work/7949154.html 
(18:47) Finally, Jill Robbins and Andrew Smith present Lesson of the Day. Today, the two explore very common informal forms of speech. Using Lesson 21 Level 1 of Let’s Learn English, Jill and Andrew explain the common structure “have to.” It sounds like “hafta.” They also talk about how native speakers use “everybody.” There are lots of examples of characters using the terms to describe common activities. https://learningenglish.voanews.com/a/lets-learn-english-lesson-21-can-you-come-to-the-party/3406732.html 
Then Caty and Mario sign off.

title: Stop-motion video created by Kids: The Ware-hedgehog
description:
This video was created by two of my English Second Language students Inka and Filip. We discussed the scenario on our lesson and what we would need. Inka directed and took the photos using an iPhone 5SE and Filip and I staged the scenes. We then put it all together during our lessons on iMovie. We learned new vocabulary by searching for different sounds that we needed for our film online. It was great to finally see the effects of our work once it was all put together. 
If you have any questions on how to create something like this on your lessons let me know in the comments!

title: Dinosaur frog, Carter and Afghanistan, AI tools for learning disabilities
description:
Caty Weaver and Mario Ritter host today's program.

First: A large frog species that lived alongside dinosaurs and is considered a "living fossil" is now losing ground in its native Chile. Climate change and human actions are damaging the creature's living environment, or habitat. John Russell reports about the situation of the helmeted water toad. https://learningenglish.voanews.com/a/large-chilean-frog-at-risk-from-climate-change/7907273.html

Next: Former American President Jimmy Carter’s aid to rebel groups in Afghanistan in 1979 started a policy that the leader who followed him, President Ronald Reagan, would continue in the 1980s. The Soviet withdrawal from Afghanistan helped lead to the collapse of the former Soviet Union. Caty Weaver and Andrew Smith report about this piece of history. (3:08) https://learningenglish.voanews.com/a/historians-remember-president-jimmy-carter-s-efforts-to-aid-afghan-rebels/7932830.html

Then: Artificial intelligence (AI) is being used to help students with visual, speech, language and hearing disabilities. Schools in the United States are developing methods for how to use AI and are trying out new applications. Jill Robbins and Mario Ritter present the subject in this week's Education Tips. (11:24) https://learningenglish.voanews.com/a/students-with-disabilities-praise-assistive-technology-using-ai/7926297.html

Finally: The Lesson of the Day. Andrew Smith and Jill Robbins base their instruction on the LE video series, Let's Learn English. Today Andrew and Jill teach about the words "enthusiastic" and "fantastic." They also go over some expressions and short words that Americans tend to say very fast. (18:08) https://learningenglish.voanews.com/a/lets-learn-english-lesson-16-where-are-you-from/3355849.html

description:

title: Chorus Waves, Free salmon, High blood pressure, Food trucks
description:
Podcast for 02/04/25 Contents:

Caty Weaver and Mario Ritter Jr. host today's program.
First: Scientists have detected bursts of plasma, called chorus waves, in an unexpected part of space. This discovery raises questions about how they were formed. Anna Matteo has the details. (1:15)
Next: A New York food bank was offered more than 18,100 kilograms of salmon. But there was a problem. The Food Bank of Central New York needed to find a way to remove about 13,000 fish from the water and then process them into fillets. They did it with the help of the business and many volunteers.  John Russell reports.
Then: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has approved a treatment to reduce severe high blood pressure. The treatment targets some nerves in the kidneys using ultrasound. Doctors think the treatment might reduce nerve signals that can affect blood pressure. Andrew Smith reports on the subject for this week's Health and Lifestyle Report. (10:06)
Finally: The Lesson of the Day. Jill Robbins and Andrew Smith base their instruction on the LE video series Let's Learn English. Today, they talk about episode 23, which focuses on food trucks and international cuisine. Learn the language of US coin money and some fast-spoken English terms. "Whaddaya" think Andrew and Jill might teach us? (17:12) 
Caty and Mario close the show.

title: Gettysburg, Power couple, Moon’s grand canyon, Homophones
description:
Bryan Lynn and Anna Matteo host today's program. 
First: Gettysburg is home to a museum and National Park honoring the Civil War battle that took place there in 1863. It was the deadliest battle of the war in which Americans fought each other. Mario Ritter tells about the famous area. (1:18) https://learningenglish.voanews.com/a/american-places-gettysburg-pennsylvania/7965779.html 
 
Then: The LE program Words and Their Stories. Anna Matteo has some expressions to describe when two people have a lot of similarities or are very close. A "power couple" might even work together. But do not read too much into that. (5:15) https://learningenglish.voanews.com/a/what-does-it-take-to-be-a-power-couple-/7963076.html 

Next: Bryan Lynn brings us the Science and Technology Report. He tells about a new study of an asteroid strike on the moon billions of years ago. The crash happened near the moon’s south pole. Researchers say it created two huge valleys, about the size of Earth’s Grand Canyon. (9:57) https://learningenglish.voanews.com/a/study-asteroid-hit-created-two-grand-canyons-on-moon/7964413.html 
 
Finally: The LE Lesson of the Day. Andrew Smith and Jill Robbins base their instruction on the LE video series, Let's Learn English. Today they teach about homophones - words that sound the same, but are spelled differently, like "cell" and "sell." title: Pet therapy, Oldest pet cemetery, Christmas in America, Dreams
description:
On today’s Christmas Day program, Caty Weaver and Mario Ritter, Jr. host the show.
Caty tells listeners what they are going to hear.
(:53)First, Bryan Lynn has a story about a group that brings horses and people together. A non-profit group in Greece uses small horses to provide treatment for sick and disabled people. But the organization is now considering its future after facing financial difficulties. The horses provide a form of therapy that offers valuable social interactions and new learning experiences for people. The treatment is sometimes called “pet therapy.” https://learningenglish.voanews.com/a/mini-horses-in-greece-bring-joy-to-sick-disabled/7904925.html
(7:22) Then, Caty has a story about a place where animals who were beloved pets are buried. Hartsdale Pet Cemetery was established in 1896 and added to the National Register of Historic Places in 2012. It is the oldest place of its kind in America. The burials can cost up to $7000. Patrons like Mark Lindenberg say it is worth it. https://learningenglish.voanews.com/a/oldest-pet-burial-ground-in-america-is-final-resting-place-for-thousands/7897363.html
(14:28) After that, Caty introduces a program about Christmas in America long ago in the first half of the 19th century. Shirley Griffith talks about a nostalgic story from Washington Irving. Steve Ember also talks about how Christmas traditions formed around the holiday that celebrated the birth of Jeses, including trees, gifts and candy. By the middle of the 1800s, American Christian groups began to ignore their religious differences over the meaning of Christmas and honored the day in special ways. Shirley and Steve, then discuss how Christmas became an official holiday and some of the music that makes the observance very special. They also hint at the beginning of Santa Claus. https://learningenglish.voanews.com/a/a-history-of-chrismas-in-america/4174019.html
(22:15) Finally, Andrew Smith and Jill Robbins present Lesson of the Day. This episode is based on Lesson 30 of Level 2 of Let’s Learn English. The episode is the final one in the series and it’s main idea is dreams. Andrew and Jill describe how the characters, including Anna Matteo, discuss their dreams for the future. They also share some wisdom about life and ask listeners about their own dreams. https://learningenglish.voanews.com/a/lets-learn-english-level-2-lesson-30/4465315.html
Then Caty and Mario sign off.

title: Everyday Grammar Video: How Does Share Fit into Sentences?
description:
JR: Hi Dr. Jill! Let’s continue our exploration of one word: share. Last time, we talked about the noun and verb forms.  
Dr. J: Perhaps now, we can add in a little more grammar. Let's start with how “share” commonly fits into sentences.  
JR: Google’s Ngram Viewer, an online database consisting of thousands of books, tells us the most common words that come before "share" are "to" and "a." The word “to” often marks the infinitive form of the verb. That’s the short word “to” along with the base form of the verb.  
Dr. J: The short word “a” is an article – a kind of determiner. It marks the beginning of a noun or noun phrase.  But you should know that Ngram Viewer also gives us an important finding: "to share" is far more common than "a share." 
JR: What that means is that we are more likely to read something like this:  
The children decided to share the blocks. 
Or, Dr. Jill didn’t want to share her pizza.
Dr. J: We are somewhat less likely to read a sentence like this: 
She bought a share of the company’s stock. 
JR: We might also ask this question: What words are likely to come after "share?" 
Dr. J: The two most common structures, at least according to Google's Ngram Viewer, are "share of" and "share the." 
JR: Now, think back to our earlier examples: 
She bought a share of the company’s stock. 
The children decided to share the blocks. 
Dr. J: Hey! Next time you have to pick up the pizza and earn your share of it! And that’s Everyday Grammar!

title: How to Pronounce: Pronouncing scientific terms - evidence
description:
Hello! I’m John Russell. 
Let’s continue our exploration of common scientific terms. 
Today we pay careful attention to an important noun: evidence. 
This term can be difficult for native speakers of many languages.
So, let’s work together to improve our pronunciation of the term. 
Evidence is the information or facts that suggest something is more likely or less likely to be true. 
We can break apart the word into its vowel and consonant sounds. 
Evidence has two vowel sounds. The first vowel sound is this:
 ɛ
The other vowel sound occurs twice. It is this vowel sound:
ə
We can now compare our vowel sounds:
There are several consonant sounds. But one of the sounds that is tricky for speakers of many languages is this:
v
To make this sound, we put our lip under our front teeth. 
You should know that this sound is a voiced consonant. That means you should be able to feel your vocal cords move when you make the sound. 
Let’s end our report with an example from a VOA Learning English report. You will hear Bryan Lynn use “evidence” in a sentence.
Scientists say they have found evidence that the smelly molecule hydrogen sulfide exists in the atmosphere of a Jupiter-like planet.  
That’s all for today! Keep up the good work.

title: English in a Minute: Head and Shoulders Above
description:
Welcome to English in a Minute! 
My shoulders and my head are both at the top of my body. So, what does it mean if something is head and shoulders above something else?
Anna: Andrew, I have found the perfect pizza. Perfect Pizza Palace! 
Andrew: That place is way too expensive. 
Anna: Maybe. But their pizza is head and shoulders above all the other pizza places in this city! And I’ve tried them all.  
Andrew: You could not… 
Anna: All.
If something is “head and shoulders above” something else, it is better than all others, or simply the best! It’s as if it is placed higher than everything around it.  
And that’s English in a Minute.

title: English in a Minute: Break the News
description:
Learn common American English idioms with English in a Minute.
Welcome to English in a Minute. News can be any information that is, well, new to someone. But what does it mean to “break the news?”  
 
Andrew: So, are you all ready for our big work trip to Brazil? I just bought a new travel shirt, travel sunglasses and this travel guidebook!  
Anna: Andrew, I hate to break the news, but you’re not traveling.  
Andrew: But, but, but… 
Anna: Budget cuts. There’s not enough money for two. But can I borrow that travel book? 

To “break the news” means to tell someone bad news – something that will make them upset or sad. Breaking the news can be a hard thing to do and so can hearing about it.

title: News Words: Illusion
description:
Welcome to the Voice of America’s News Words.                 

A museum in Miami, Florida specializes in works of art that stretch the imagination. 
                                         
ILLUSION                   

The Miami Paradox Museum is one of several paradox museums across the world. More than 70 of its displays produce optical illusions worthy of a photograph. The museum explains the math and science behind each illusion.
An illusion is anything that is false or not real but that seems to be true or real. 
An optical illusion tricks your eyes to make you think you see something that is not present or that looks different in reality.

title: Everyday Grammar TV: Personification in Take me Home, Country Roads’
description:
JR: In our last lesson we talked about metaphor in the song, “Take Me Home, Country Roads.” Dr. Jill, did you notice any other writing techniques while listening to the song during your long drive to West Virginia with Anna Matteo?
Dr. J: I sure did! I noticed that the song uses personification. 
JR: Let’s see, that’s when you talk about a nonliving thing as if it is a human. 
Dr. J: When we use personification, we may use pronouns like “she” or “her” to talk about objects. Listen to this line about the land of West Virginia referred to as “her.” 
All my memories gather 'round her
JR: The singer is also saying the land is like a woman the miner remembers. 
Dr. J: You can hear that in this line about the mountain’s voice calling the singer. Note the use of the pronouns “her” and “she.”
I hear her voice in the morning hour, she calls me
JR: And in our last lesson, we told you about the line comparing the state to a mother:
West Virginia, mountain mamma
That is another example of personification.
Dr. J: I’ve heard you talk about your car this way – with the pronoun “she.”
JR: Oh, do you mean, “My old Ford wouldn’t start this morning – I think she doesn’t like cold weather.”
Dr. J: That shows how much you love your car, John.
JR: Almost as much as I love grammar!
Dr. J: And that’s Everyday Grammar TV!

title: English in a Minute: On the Ball
description:
Welcome to English in a Minute! Some people use a large ball for exercise. Is that what to get “on the ball” means?   
Andrew: Hi Anna! How has your day been?  
Anna: Great! Very great! Very productive! I finished three reports and have only one more to do!  
Andrew: Wow, you are on the ball! How did you do them so fast?  
Anna: Coffee! Lots of coffee. Do you want some? I’ll get it. I’d love more coffee. Thank you!  
Andrew: Uh, sure. But maybe not that much coffee.  
Someone who is “on the ball” finishes work quickly and ahead of time.  We can also say a person should “get on the ball” when they need to work better or faster. And that’s English in a Minute!

title: Everyday Grammar Video: Understanding Share as a Noun and Verb
description:
JR: Hi Dr. Jill! I have a tricky question for you.  
Dr. J: Hi John! Let’s hear the question.  
JR: What is one word that we often read in the business section of a newspaper? We also use the same word when we talk about gatherings with family or friends. 
Dr. J: Hmmm... The verb discuss? Or perhaps the noun discussion? 
JR: That’s a great answer... but not the one I had in mind.  
DR. J [laughs]: What did you have in mind, John? 
JR: Share. We use it both as a noun and as a verb.  
Dr. J: Yes, that’s correct. And we can learn a lot about grammar from exploring one word.   
JR: Remember at lunch today when we had a pizza. 
Dr. J: Yeah, I cut it up and shared it with you.
JR: But you only gave me two slices and you ate six slices! Your share was much bigger than my share!
Dr J: But I was hungry! I had to go out and walk to the shop to pick up the pizza!
JR: Anyway, we can use this to teach about the noun and verb forms for “share.” 
Dr. J: Both the noun and verb forms suggest the idea of division or splitting something. 
JR: So, the noun form, as in “a share” can involve value or ownership that is divided into parts. For example, a person might buy a share of a company. This means that a person is buying partial ownership of the business. 
Dr. J:  Or your share might be slices of a pizza. And I used the verb form when I said, “I shared the pizza with you.”
JR: Thanks for sharing. But next time please give me an equal share. 
Dr. J: I will! And that’s Everyday Grammar!

title: News Words: Unanimous
description:
Welcome to the Voice of America’s News Words.  
Florida Senator Marco Rubio was recently sworn in as American Secretary of State.
UNANIMOUS   
The secretary of state, or the country’s chief diplomat, was appointed by the president and approved by a unanimous vote in the Senate. Secretary Rubio said the president’s foreign policy is centered on the advancement of the country’s national interest.  
Unanimous means in complete agreement. In other words, all the senators voted the same. In a U.S. criminal jury trial, a unanimous decision is required to judge someone guilty or not guilty.

title: Birdwatching in Alabama, Spread thin, ISS stay, Prediction
description:

(1:14) First, John Russell has a story about a natural area in the American South. Wheeler National Wildlife Center in the southeastern state of Alabama has become popular with birdwatchers. (7:27) Then Anna presents her weekly program on English language expressions. This week on Words and Their Stories, Anna talks about expressions describing taking on too much. title: English in a Minute: The Bottom Line
description:
Welcome to English in a Minute! This piece of paper has lines at the top, middle and bottom.

But what does “the bottom line” mean? 
AM: Andrew, did you watch the baseball game last night? 
AS: Yes, I did. And I saw us lose, again. We need some new players.  
AM: Well, they’re getting better. And they tried really hard! 
AS: Yeah, they try hard, but the bottom line is, you have to hit the ball to win.
AM: They weren’t hitting.
The bottom line means the most basic or important thing to consider in a situation.
"Bottom line” can also be used to mean the final result or outcome. 
And that’s English in a Minute!

title: Everyday Grammar Video: Goodbye in Formal Conversations
description:
JR: In an earlier lesson we talked about ways to say goodbye. We only had time for the formal ways, like “Goodbye” and “Have a good day.”
Dr.J: Today, we want to teach some informal ways to part from a friend. 
JR: If you think you will see them soon, you might say, “See you soon” or “See ya’ soon” 
Dr.J: When we speak informally, we often used the reduced vowel, or schwa, which sounds like ‘uh.”  In writing, you might see this written with “ya” as in “See ya later” or “See ya’ around!”
JR: The structure for these expressions is Verb (with an optional Preposition) + you + time
      Example: See you later
DrJ: One example with a preposition is, “Talk to you later.”
JR: So we might say, “see you tomorrow” or “catch you next week.”
Dr.J: Sometime we just use “until” with “later” or another time word. For example, “Until tomorrow.”
JR: I’ve heard people just say, “later.”
Dr.J: And sometimes we are saying goodbye to someone we don’t expect to see again soon.  In that case, we wish them well.
JR: At the goodbye party for Mary, I heard some of those. One was “Take care of yourself and stay in touch.”
Dr.J: Right. If someone is leaving on a trip, you can wish them a safe journey, with “Have a safe trip!”
JR: Or we can say, “Drive safely.”
Dr.J: Well. I have to go now, John. As our friend Anna says, “Until next time!”
JR: Later, Jill! And that’s Everyday Grammar!

title: Super Bowl history, Regardless, Fall of the House of Usher Part 2
description:
On this program, Caty Weaver and Mario Ritter, Jr. host the show. Caty tells listeners what they are going to hear.

(:50) First, Caty has a story about a big yearly event in America. Known as “The Big Game,” the Super Bowl has become a major part of American life. The first Super Bowl took place in January 1967. In Sunday’s game, the Kansas City Chiefs will try to defeat the Philadelphia Eagles to win their third championship in a row.

(5:50) Then, Jill Robbins and John Russell present our Everyday Grammar program. This week, Jill and John examine patterns in English. They discuss sentence structure that is common in academic writing. Today’s lesson looks at intransitive verbs. What are intransitive verbs and how are they used? Intransitive verbs do not need an object. But they are often linked with things like adverbial clauses or phrases which give additional information. Listen and learn a lot about these structures that are more important to writing than you think.

(13:51) This week on Ask a Teacher, Andrew Smith answers a question from Ramatoulaye in Senegal about the difference between the words “regarding” and “regardless.” Andrew also explains the use of the verb “regard.” Examples show how these terms are best used and how they help speaks talk about things that might or might not affect what they are trying to explain or talk about.

(18:32) Finally, part two of Edgar Allan Poe’s “The Fall of the House of Usher” gives the history of the sad owner of an old house in a mysterious place. A visiting childhood friend bears witness to Usher’s story and to the apparent death of his twin sister. But the horror builds with small details that increase the expectation of a terrible end.
Then, Caty and Mario sign off.

description:

That could open the way for mineral exploration. https://learningenglish.voanews.com/a/greenland-holds-important-position-in-a-warming-world/7935035.html

The BepiColombo spacecraft with orbiters from the European Space Agency and Japan’s space agency flew close to the north pole of the Solar System’s innermost planet. Mercury is closest to the sun, but its poles are extremely cold. Scientists theorize that deep craters in the planet’s polar areas could hold water ice. https://learningenglish.voanews.com/a/european-and-japanese-spacecraft-examines-mercury-s-pole-/7935379.html

title: How to Pronounce: Scientific Terms - Accuracy
description:
Hello! I’m John Russell. 
Let’s continue our exploration of scientific terms. 
Developing our ability to pronounce scientific words can help us discuss the earth sciences, social sciences, and more. 
Today, we pay special attention to the word “accuracy.”
Accuracy is a noun. It is a measure of how close something is to its true value. 
So, let’s try to be ... accurate with our pronunciation of “accuracy.”
To start, accuracy has stress on the very beginning of the word. We can show that by clapping on the stressed part of the word. 
Watch, listen, and repeat:
Accuracy
Accuracy 
Accuracy
We have the stress at the beginning of the word. What else do we need to know?
We can divide the word into small parts and focus on saying the  vowels and consonants very clearly. 
Listen and repeat after me:
A (first vowel)
A 
Kyə
Kyə
Rə
Rə
Sē
Sē
Let’s put it all together:
Accuracy 
Accuracy 
Accuracy 
We can end by listening to a clip from VOA Learning English’s 
Bryan Lynn use the term in a science and technology story:
https://learningenglish.voanews.com/a/google-ai-found-breast-cancer-with-99-percent-accuracy/4627357.html
“Google says it created a mathematical algorithm that greatly improves this accuracy rate.”
OR 
But it is hopeful that “deep learning technologies and well-designed clinical tools” can be continually developed to improve accuracy and availability for patients worldwide.

That’s all for today! Keep up the good work.

title: Everyday Grammar TV: A Gift-giving Sentence Pattern
description:
JR: Hi Dr. Jill!  
Dr. J: Hi John! You know, this is a big gift-giving season in the United States.  
JR: Not for me! You know I don’t give gifts. I do enjoy receiving them, however.  
Dr. J: That’s not a very nice attitude, John.  
JR: I’m joking... well, I’m kind of joking ... 
Dr. J: For today’s lesson, we might explore a common sentence pattern we use to describe the gifts that we gave.  
JR: Like the transitive verb followed by two noun phrases.  
Dr. J: Sure, that’s a great example.  
JR: Transitive verbs take a direct object. The direct object receives the action of the verb. The direct object is our first noun phrase.  
Dr. J: The indirect object – the person who receives the direct object - is our second noun phrase.  
JR: Let’s take an example. 
Bob gave his son a ukelele.  
Dr. J: Here, we have the verb “give.” The direct object is “a ukelele” What did Bob give? He gave a ukelele. Who is going to receive the ukelele? His son. In this case, “his son” is the indirect object. 
JR: Here’s another example: 
Susan bought her mother a sweater. 
Dr. J: Note that this time we have the verb “buy.” The direct object is “a sweater.” What did Susan buy? A sweater. Who is going to receive the sweater? Her mother. In this example, “her mother” is the indirect object.  
JR: You know, all of these nice example sentences make me want to give gifts. Maybe we can end with a final example:  
I am giving Dr. Jill a Christmas gift. (hands jill a gift bag) 
Dr. J: Wow, thanks, John! (opening bag) It’s a hat! Just what I needed! And that’s Everyday Grammar TV.

title: Women on motorcycles, Iodine, Resolutions, People watching
description:

(1:05) First, Jill Robbins has a story about women aiming to learn new skills in Pakistan. A driving school program in Lahore, Pakistan called Women on Wheels is helping women learn to drive motorcycles. Women in the program say it has given them more freedom of movement as they are less dependent on men to take them places. https://learningenglish.voanews.com/a/program-helps-pakistani-women-learn-to-ride-gain-independence/7918883.html
(4:54) After that, John Russell has a report about a necessary nutrient. Although researchers say most Americans get enough iodine through their diet, some doctors report rising rates of deficiency among some populations, including women and children. https://learningenglish.voanews.com/a/doctors-concerned-about-return-of-iodine-deficiency/7932629.html
(11:35)  Then, Anna Matteo has a story about a popular tradition that begins on New Year’s Day. New Year’s resolutions are usually meant to bring a change lasting all year. In today’s Health & Lifestyle report, experts share advice about keeping New Year’s resolutions. They say January can be a good time for self-improvement but waiting for spring to come might be just as good. The experts advise to “start small” which means to choose a goal that is not big. Another bit of advice is “be realistic.” That means making goals that are able to be reached. The report gives a lot of advice for sticking with your resolutions. https://learningenglish.voanews.com/a/advice-on-successfully-keeping-new-year-s-promises/7930227.html

Then they advise not to judge people by their appearance. They also explore the ideas of socioeconomic qualities and hierarchy. https://learningenglish.voanews.com/a/lets-learn-english-lesson-15-i-love-people-watching/3343720.html

title: News Words: Deter
description:
Welcome to the Voice of America’s News Words.                 
In Kenya, some of the world’s smallest insects are controlling some of the world’s largest creatures. 

DETER                  

The group Save the Elephants is helping farmers near Tsavo National Park who say the elephants are destroying their crops. They use African honeybees to deter the huge animals who fear the tiny insects. 

To deter is to restrain or prevent someone from taking action, usually through fear of the result of such action. 
For example, posting an armed guard at a store could deter stealing.

title: Everyday Grammar Video: Goodbye In Informal Conversations
description:
JR: In an earlier lesson we talked about ways to say goodbye. We only had time for the formal ways, like “Goodbye” and “Have a good day.” 

Dr.J: Today, we want to teach some informal ways to part from a friend.  

JR: If you think you will see them soon, you might say, “See you soon” or “See ya’ soon”  

Dr.J: When we speak informally, we often used the reduced vowel, or schwa, which sounds like ‘uh.”  In writing, you might see this written with “ya” as in “See ya later” or “See ya’ around!” 

JR: The structure for these expressions is Verb (with an optional Preposition) + you + time 

Example: See you later 

DrJ: One example with a preposition is, “Talk to you later.” 

JR: So we might say, “see you tomorrow” or “catch you next week.” 

Dr.J: Sometime we just use “until” with “later” or another time word. For example, “Until tomorrow.” 

JR: I’ve heard people just say, “later.” 

Dr.J: And sometimes we are saying goodbye to someone we don’t expect to see again soon.  In that case, we wish them well. 

JR: At the goodbye party for Mary, I heard some of those. One was “Take care of yourself and stay in touch.” 

Dr.J: Right. If someone is leaving on a trip, you can wish them a safe journey, with “Have a safe trip!” 

JR: Or we can say, “Drive safely.” 

Dr.J: Well. I have to go now, John. As our friend Anna says, “Until next time!” 

JR: Later, Jill! And that’s Everyday Grammar!

title: How to Pronounce: Pronouncing scientific terms - inference
description:
Hello! I’m John Russell. 
Let’s continue our exploration of common scientific terms. 
Today’s word is inference. 
An inference is some kind of opinion or conclusion. This opinion or conclusion is a result of facts or evidence that is closely examined. 

Inference can be a difficult word for speakers of many languages – Persian, some Indian languages, and others. Why?
Part of it comes down to the “r” sound – one of the middle sounds in “inference.”
I’ll explain. 

The American “r” can be tricky.  
There are a couple ways to form it.
I’ll tell you the method I use while pronouncing the word. 
For this method, you want to have the back of your tongue do the work. You need to press the sides of your tongue up against the back teeth. You do not need to curl your tongue. 
You can’t really see inside my mouth, so we will have to use our imaginations a little. 
What else do you need to know about inference? 
We generally stress the beginning of the word. We can show this by clapping when we say the word. 
/ˈɪnfərəns/
One last point. Inference has two vowel sounds. The first vowel sound goes like this:

title: English in a Minute: Fair and Square
description:
English in a Minute: Fair and Square

Welcome to English in a Minute. We all like to be treated fairly. But what about being treated squarely? Let’s learn how to use the idiom “fair and square.” 
 
Andrew: Anna, where have you been? I lost you in the crowd.  
Anna: I was playing games! I’m really good at carnival games! 
Andrew: I see that! You really won a lot of stuffed animals. Are you sure you didn’t cheat?   
Anna: No! I won them fair and square! And they’re all mine. All mine!
Hahaha…!

“Fair and square” describes winning something in an honest way and without any doubt. The expression is a fun one to say because it rhymes –- fair and square!

title: Drinking less, Parker Solar probe, Jack Frost
description:
On this podcast, Bryan Lynn and Anna Matteo host the show. Anna tells listeners what they are going to hear.
(1:14) First, Andrew Smith reports on recent finding about drinking alcohol. People once thought moderate drinking had benefits for the heart. But new research methods show this might not be the case. A growing number of public health experts now advise people to drink as little as possible to improve health. Earlier this month, U.S. Surgeon General Dr. Vivek Murthy called for changing his agency’s existing health warning on alcoholic drinks to include cancer risks. Such a change would require approval from Congress. https://learningenglish.voanews.com/a/how-does-drinking-alcohol-affect-your-health-/7930063.html
(7:28) Then, Bryan Lynn reports on a NASA spacecraft that is studying the sun. NASA said on December 24 that the Parker Solar Probe got closer to our star, the sun, than any past exploration vehicle has. The spacecraft, launched in 2018, has been studying the sun’s corona and the solar wind in detail. https://learningenglish.voanews.com/a/nasa-says-spacecraft-made-closest-ever-pass-to-sun/7932240.html

(13:20) After that, Anna presents another Words and Their Stories program. This week, Anna talks about a “person” English speakers talk about when the weather gets really cold. Jack Frost is an imaginary creature. If we believe the stories, he is responsible for winter's cold weather. Of course, we believe science. But we still use his name when temperatures drop below freezing. Read this story to learn how to talk about Jack Frost. https://learningenglish.voanews.com/a/the-story-of-jack-frost-/7932530.html

(19:06) Finally, Andrew returns with Jill Robbins on Lesson of the Day. The two describe in detail the use of tag questions. They use Lesson 15, Level 1 of Let’s Learn English to talk about how people describe and talk about other people. Tag questions are important ways people confirm information they share. “It’s a nice day, isn’t it?” is an example of a tag question Jill and Andrew tell us. They also talk about guessing where people come from and mention the word stereotype. https://learningenglish.voanews.com/a/lets-learn-english-lesson-15-i-love-people-watching/3343720.html
After that, Anna and Bryan sign off.

title: How to Pronounce: Scientific Terms - Prediction
description:
Hello! I’m John Russell. 
Let’s continue exploring scientific terms. Mastering these terms can help us discuss the earth sciences, social sciences, and more.
Today, we pay careful attention to the word “prediction.”
A prediction is a statement about a future event or outcome. Prediction is a central term to the scientific method. 
Let’s start by noting that prediction ends with the letters –tion. 
This is a common ending known as a suffix.
When we have nouns such as prediction that end in the suffix –tion, American have a general formula we follow to pronounce the word. 
The general formula is this:
Stress the syllable that comes before the –tion ending. 
That might sound a little complex, but the word “prediction” can help us. 
When we practice saying words, it can be useful to clap on stressed syllables. This way, we know that we are saying certain parts of the word in the way that a native speaker would. 
We will work together to develop this skill. I will clap on the stressed syllable. Note that the stressed syllable occurs before the –tion ending. 
Prediction 
Prediction 
Prediction 
Now let’s listen to how a native English speaker might use “prediction” in a sentence. 
Here is VOA Learning English’s Bryan Lynn using the term “prediction” in a Science and Technology report. 
https://learningenglish.voanews.com/a/ai-can-improve-weather-predictions-if-used-with-traditional-methods/7826267.html
The ECMWF technology is called the Artificial Intelligence/Integrated Forecasting System (AIFS). The group describes the system as a “data-driven" forecasting model. It is designed to make many predictions quickly, including for extreme events involving powerful storms and heatwaves.

title: Everyday Grammar TV: Open-ended Questions about Gifts
description:
Dr. J: Hi John! 
JR: Hi Dr. Jill! 
Dr. J: We are now in between two major American holidays: Thanksgiving and Christmas. This is the most important time of the year for getting gifts for others. 
JR: Unless you are like me. I don’t give gifts. 
Dr. J: Why not? Do you have a moral or religious reason for not giving gifts?
JR: No, I’m just cheap and unpleasant. 
Dr. J secretly to camera: He is cheap, but he’s one of the nicest guys I know!”
Dr. J: Well, most Americans give gifts. And most Americans ask questions about the gifts that others would like. So, let’s talk about some of the elements we use to ask these questions. 
John: Our main elements are:
1. A question word 
2. Modals or a helping verb
3. A main verb
4. The short word “for” 
5. Nouns or noun phrases
Dr. J: The question word “what” is commonly used.  “Like” or “want” are two of the most common examples of main verbs. 
Dr. J: Let’s put it all together. We might ask a question like this: 
What                        would   John      like         for   Christmas?
[question word] [modal][noun][main verb][for][noun]
JR: Or you might ask this: 
What                 does     John want     for Christmas?
[question word] [do] [noun] [like] [for] [noun]
JR: Note that we can replace our final noun with almost any holiday or celebration. So, you might ask “What does John want for his birthday?” or “What would John like for his birthday?”
Dr. J: The problem with these examples is that John is always thinking of himself. That’s not the Christmas spirit, John. You should be thinking of others! 
JR: “Oh, so I should give this example: What does Dr. Jill want for Christmas?” 
Dr. J: That’s better! I need a warm hat. And that’s Everyday Grammar TV.

title: How to Pronounce:  Pronouncing scientific terms – hypothesis
description:
Hello! I’m John Russell. 
Let’s continue our exploration of scientific terms. 
Today, we explore a word that can be difficult for native speakers of many languages – Persian, Russian, Japanese, and more. 
What is this term?
Hypothesis. 
A hypothesis is some kind of idea or suggestion that is made for the purpose of testing. 
Hypothesis is a central term in the scientific method.
Why might it be difficult to pronounce?
There is one consonant sound that is difficult for speakers of many languages.  It is the –th- sound. 
We make the sound by putting our tongue between our lips, like this:
Then we blow out air and make sure that our vocal cords do not move. You can use your fingers to check, like this:
What else should you know about the word hypothesis? 
English speakers put stress on the second part of the word. We do not stress the beginning or the end of the word. 
We can clap on the stressed part of the word to clarify this point. 
The work we have done today is very exact and specific. But the next time you read about or discuss scientific issues, you can have more confidence that you are pronouncing the word “hypothesis” correctly. 
That’s all for today! 
Keep up the good work.

title: English in a Minute: No Brainer
description:
Caty: Welcome to English in a Minute! We have to use our brains to think. So, what does the expression, “no brainer” mean? 
 
Andrew: Hey, did you watch the new episode of Catch a Criminal? 
 
Anna: Yeah, but it was such a no-brainer! The police found a gun and all the money in David’s house!  
 
Andrew: Well, what if David has a twin who lives with him? 
 
Anna: The police would know if David had a twin brother. 
 
Andrew: Well, what if they don’t know? 
 
Anna: Then they are really bad at their jobs! 
 
A no brainer is something that requires little thought or is obvious.  
It also means it is easy to make the right choice. And that’s English in Minute!

title: News Words: Brain Rot
description:
Welcome to the Voice of America’s News Words.                
Oxford University Press has released its word of the year for 2024.
BRAIN ROT         
The phrase “brain rot” was chosen because it represents an important idea from the past year. 
Oxford defines brain rot as the supposed weakening of a person’s intelligence or mental state, especially as the result of watching or reading a large amount of meaningless material, especially online.
The Oxford Languages president said brain rot speaks to the perceived dangers of virtual life and how people use their free time.

title: English in a Minute: Pie in the Sky
description:
elcome to English in a Minute.   

Pie is a delicious dessert! And there are so many different flavors, like cherry, lemon, banana cream! But what could the idiom “pie in the sky” mean?  

Anna: Pedro is finally moving to Hollywood to follow his acting dream.    

Andrew: He’s been talking about that for years. His plans are just pie in the sky.   

Anna: His YouTube channel has over four million subscribers!   

Andrew: Four million? Hmm. - 

Anything “pie in the sky” could be great but probably won’t happen. As an adjective, “pie in the sky" describes dreams, goals, or plans that are unlikely to become reality.

title: Everyday Grammar TV: Metaphor in ‘Take me Home, Country Roads’
description:
JR: Dr. Jill, I hear you took a little trip over the holidays.
Dr. J: Yes, I went with Anna Matteo to visit West Virginia.
JR: That sounds like fun! Did you drive together?
Dr. J: Yes, and all the way we sang that song, “Take Me Home, Country Roads!”
JR: Wow! And you’re still friends? That’s a long time to be singing one song.
Dr. J: (Laughing) Yes, of course! And I thought of what great lessons we can teach with it, too!
JR: Let me guess. I think the song uses special writing techniques known as literary devices. Is that right?
Dr. J: Correct. One of them is metaphor – comparing two things without saying “is like.”  Let me give you an example. The song begins, “Almost heaven, West Virginia.”
JR: That is saying that West Virginia is like Heaven, a good place. It’s a metaphor because the writer wants to compare West Virginia to the best place possible.
Dr. J: But the important thing to remember is that metaphor does not use the word “like.”
JR: Are there any other metaphors you found in the song?
Dr. J: Yes, how about this one: “West Virginia, mountain mamma, Take me home, country roads.”
JR: The writer is comparing the mountain to a mother.
Dr. J: I think that’s because the mountain is welcoming and familiar like a mother. You know, John we use metaphors all the time, not just in songs and poetry.
JR: I’ve got one now – we are two peas in a pod because we both like grammar! [graphic of peas in a pod] 
Dr. J: And Everyday Grammar TV is a breath of fresh air! And that’s Everyday Grammar TV.

title: Everyday Grammar Video: Talking Kindly About Mental Illness
description:
JR: In our last lesson, we talked about the best words and language to use when talking about mental health and mental illness.
Dr. J: We said that it’s best to use person-centered language. Here is one structure: 
Subject + verb live + preposition with + noun form of illness.
JR: An example is 
Bill lives with depression.
Dr. J: Another way you can talk about mental illness is to use this structure: 
Subject + verb have + noun form of illness.
JR: Using that form, we would say, 
Amy has anxiety.
Dr. J: It’s important to remember that we avoid using informal words like “crazy” to talk about a person with a mental illness. That kind of language can be harmful.
JR: Experts say using such words can lead to stigma. Stigma is a set of negative beliefs that a culture has about something. 
Dr. J: Stigma can prevent people from seeking help with their own mental illnesses. And before we go, I think we should talk about ways to have good mental health. 
JR: Good idea, Dr. Jill. I know for me, doing something creative like making music helps to keep me happy. 
Dr. J: And I enjoy my volunteer work – helping other people makes me feel good. 
JR: Some other ways are to exercise or learn breathing methods, or to just take a break from your routine.
Dr. J: Hey, that’s great advice. Let’s take a break now!
JR: And that’s Everyday Grammar!

title: Birds of prey, Einstein ring, Yellowstone, Superlatives
description:
On this program, Bryan Lynn and Anna Matteo host the show. Bryan tells listeners what they are going to hear.
(2:19) First, Anna presents Words and Their Stories. This week, she explains ways that English speakers might describe someone who is sharp or who has good vision. Some birds, called raptors, are known for their extremely sharp vision. Eagles, hawks, and owls can see their prey from very far away. Learn how we use these birds in many English expressions. For example, hear how “a bird’s eye view” and “eagle-eyed” are used in everyday speech. https://learningenglish.voanews.com/a/don-t-miss-a-thing-with-eagle-eyes-/7963085.html
(8:25) Then, Bryan reports on a discovery in space that surprised researchers. Scientists say Europe’s Euclid space telescope has discovered a bright ring of light around a nearby galaxy. The light, known as an Einstein ring, results when the light of a more distant galaxy bends around a nearer galaxy forming a circle of light. https://learningenglish.voanews.com/a/european-telescope-discovers-einstein-ring-in-nearby-galaxy/7972838.html
(15:21) Next, Andrew Smith tells listeners about a wild and special place in the western United States. Mainly in the state of Wyoming, Yellowstone National Park was the first and remains one of the largest of America’s great parks. It is home to the largest collection of wild animals in the lower 48 states. It is also an active volcanoe and it is famous for its geothermal activity. https://learningenglish.voanews.com/a/yellowstone-the-world-s-first-national-park/7974034.html
(20:13) Finally, Andrew joins Jill Robbins for another Lesson of the Day. The explore the details of using superlative: things that are the biggest, smallest, best and worst. In Lesson 30, Level 1 of Let’s Learn English, Anna and her friends use superlatives to describe a seafood market in Washington, D.C. Jill and Andrew talk about some examples of superlatives like “freshest” and “oldest,” but they note you cannot say “deliciousest.” So there are some rules to remember. https://learningenglish.voanews.com/a/lets-learn-english-lesson-30-rolling-river/3522798.html 
Then Bryan and Anna sign off.

title: Red dye ban, Celtic society, Meta fact check change, Objectivity
description:
Caty Weaver and Mario Ritter Jr. host today's program.
First: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration is ordering food and drug makers to remove a coloring called Red No. 3 from food products. The chemical had long been banned in skin products but still is used in some foods. Jill Robbins reports.
(1:03) https://learningenglish.voanews.com/a/red-coloring-linked-to-cancer-risk-banned-in-us-foods/7944856.html
Then: Researchers recently published a study on the Celtic society in England that existed more than 2000 years ago. They say, Celtic men might have been more likely to join their wives’ social group, a finding that conflicts with earlier studies of similar societies in other places. John Russell has the details. title: English in a Minute: A Clean Slate
description:
A Clean Slate
Welcome to English in a Minute!
 In a classroom, the chalkboard is also called a slate. It’s important to clean it before starting a new lesson. So, does “clean slate” relate to teaching?  
AS: I love the start of the new year! It’s a great time to start fresh. Make a new start.
AM: Me too! This year, I’m going to start with a clean slate and give up bad habits.   
AS: Like eating donuts and drinking too much coffee?   
AM: No. No, other bad habits.    
A clean slate means a new start or beginning. This phrase comes from the use of chalk and slates in classrooms. A teacher could start a new lesson with a clean slate.  
And that’s English in a Minute!

title: English in a Minute: Hold Your Horses
description:
Welcome to English in a Minute!
Caty: Horses are big and strong. Riding them takes skill and strength. So, is the idiom “hold your horses” about controlling horses? 

Anna: Oh! Andrew, can you help me with this box?
Andrew: Just a second. I’m almost done.
Anna: Andrew, the box!
Andrew: I’m on the last page.
Anna: It’s really heavy! 
Andrew: Hold your horses! What’s in the box?
Anna: Horses!

Caty: “Hold your horses” is a way of telling someone to wait, to be patient. It’s very informal. And depending on how you say it, it could sound rude!

title: How to Pronounce: Science and Technology: Clapping and Syllable Stress
description:
Hello! I’m John Russell. 
One of the great things about language learning is that we can find educational value in almost anything. 
Today’s lesson, which continues our science and technology theme, will show you how. 
Let’s start with listening to part of a report from VOA Learning English’s Bryan Lynn. 
https://learningenglish.voanews.com/a/study-moon-s-thin-atmosphere-likely-formed-by-meteorite-strikes/7736449.html

Scientists say new examinations of soil collected on the moon suggest its atmosphere might have been created by repeated meteorite strikes.
Let’s pay careful attention to the last few words you heard: repeated meteorite strikes. These are not necessarily the easiest words to pronounce. 
We can take the group of words and do a kind of game. The goal is to improve our sense of how English words sound when put together. 
What we can do is clap on the parts of the words that we need to say louder. In other words, we clap on the parts of the words that are stressed. This clapping will permit us to create a kind of rhythm. We start slowly and then increase our speed. 
Listen and repeat after me: 
RePeated MeteoRite Strike
RePeated MeteoRite Strike
ri-ˈpē-təd  
ˈmē-tē-ə-ˌrīt  
ˈstrīk  

Now, we can slowly increase our speed. 
RePeated MeteoRite Strike
RePeated MeteoRite Strike

And if we really want a challenge, we can go very fast. 
RePeated MeteoRite Strike
RePeated MeteoRite Strike

I don’t know about you, but I’m tired after doing this activity. 

What we have done today is to develop our sense of the rhythm of English. You can do this kind of activity with almost anything. 
Poetry and limericks in particular can be fun, but really any kind of language can be useful. 
That’s all for today! Keep up the good work.

title: English in a Minute: Strike a Chord
description:
Welcome to English in a Minute.  
When you “strike a chord” in music, you play several notes at the same time.  So, are Anna and Andrew going to play music? I hope so!  
Anna: I love Amelia Earhart. Her life really struck a chord with me.   
Andrew: Really? But she was a pilot. And you’re afraid of flying.  
Anna: Oh! No, her flying career didn’t strike a chord. She loved hot chocolate. And so do I!  
When something strikes a chord with you, it causes a strong reaction, usually because you identify with it. Striking a chord can also mean that you’re reminded of something familiar.

title: How to Pronounce: Pronouncing scientific terms - method
description:

Hello! I’m John Russell. 
Today we continue our exploration of scientific terms. 
We will pay close attention to a term that can be difficult for speakers of many languages – Russian, French, Persian, and more. 
What is this word?
Method
A method is a systematic process for doing something. 
Why might this term be difficult to pronounce?
There are two reasons:
1. The consonant –th-
2. The two different vowel sounds
Let’s explore each in turn. 
We pronounce the –th-  like this:
We put out lip between our teeth and breathe out. Your vocal cords should not move. We can practice like this:
[example]
For the vowel sounds, we need to carefully differentiate between them. 
The first vowel sound is this:
ˈme-thəd 
The second vowel sound is this:
ˈme-thəd
Now let’s say both of the vowel sounds:
We will now say the entire word together:
Method 
Method.

title: How to Pronounce: Possessive Forms in Science and Technology
description:
Hello! I’m John Russell. 
We will continue our science and technology theme by listening to a VOA Learning English Science and Technology report from Bryan Lynn: 
The American space agency NASA explains the moon’s atmosphere is “very thin and weak.”
https://learningenglish.voanews.com/a/study-moon-s-thin-atmosphere-likely-formed-by-meteorite-strikes/7736449.html
I’d like to draw your attention to a few words: the moon’s atmosphere. 
We have an article, the word “the,” the possessive noun “moon’s,” and the noun “atmosphere.”
We have these individual words that together form a piece of language known as a noun phrase. 
This noun phrase can teach you an important idea about pronunciation. 
In English, we spell the possessive form with an “’s.” In our example, it is at the end of the word “moon.”
But even though we spell the possessive form with an “’s,” we pronounce it in this case with a sound that is like this:
Z
Moon
Moon’s 
What would our noun phrase sound like if we did not pronounce it like a native speaker? What if we used a different sound?
It might sound like this:
The moon’s atmosphere
Our goal is to sound more like a native speaker. So, we need to be able to produce the distinction between these two sounds:
S
Z
The difference is this: 
S is voiceless 
Z is voiced
But we want to sound more like native speakers. So let’s work together to pronounce this noun phrase. 
We will go slowly and then more quickly. 
The moon’s atmosphere
The moon’s atmosphere
The moon’s atmosphere
That’s all for today! Keep up the good work.

title: English in a Minute: Stuck in a Rut
description:
English in a Minute: Stuck in a Rut

Caty: Welcome to English in a Minute! A rut in a dirt road can make wheels get stuck. But what does it mean if a person is “stuck in a rut?” 
 
Anna: Uh…Andrew, why are you wearing that wig? 
Andrew: I know it looks funny, but I feel like I’ve been stuck in a rut. I’m just trying to change things up and feel more creative and different! 
Anna: Got it! Is it working? 
Andrew: I think it’s just making my head hot.  
 
Caty: To be “stuck in a rut” means you feel like you do the same thing over and over and need a change. But maybe that is not the change Andrew needs.

title: Everyday Grammar Video: Population
description:
JR: Hi Dr. Jill! I’m thinking of a noun we use to talk about people on Earth. Can you guess what that noun is?
Dr. J: Humanity?
JR: That’s a good guess, but not the one I had in mind. 
Dr. J: What noun were you thinking of?
JR: Population. It is a noun that means the number of people and (or) animals living in an area. We might talk about the population of the planet Earth, the population of a city, and so on. 
Dr. J: That makes sense. When we talk about nouns, we often describe them as being either count nouns or noncount nouns. 
JR: That’s right. We can make count nouns plural by adding an –s. We do not make noncount nouns plural. 
Dr. J: English speakers commonly use “population” as a countable noun. 
JR: Let’s consider some examples to clarify these points. 
You might say “Researchers predict the world’s population will increase next year.”
We use the singular form because we are talking about all the people who live in the world – one very large group!
Dr. J: But we can also make “population” plural by adding an –s. 
JR: In this case, we might use other terms to show that we are talking about different groups. For example, you might read a news report that says this:
Overweight and elderly populations are at greater risk of developing the illness. 
Dr. J: We used the plural form “populations” because we are talking about all of the members of two different groups – overweight people and elderly people. We can also use population to talk about groups of animals. For example,
Bird and reptile populations are shrinking in North America.
JR: And that’s Everyday Grammar.

title: Everyday Grammar Video: 'Population' in Sentences
description:
JR: Hi Dr. Jill! We should continue talking about the noun “population.” It’s such a useful term to talk about both people and animals. 
Dr. Jr: Hi John. That’s a fine idea. We can start by thinking about how we use “population” in sentences. 
JR: Population is a noun. If you have followed our lessons, you can probably guess that determiners – words that show if a noun is specific or general – are likely to come before “population.”
Dr. J: We can check an online database for more information. Google’s Ngram Viewer, for example, tells us that the word “the” is the most commonly used word before “population.”
JR: Grammar books say that “the” is an article. And articles are a kind of determiner. 
Dr. J: So, you are very likely to hear or read something like this:
Experts said the population declined by 1 percent.
JR: What might be the most commonly used words after the noun population? 
Dr. J: Google’s Ngram Viewer tells us that the short word “of” is the most common by far.
JR: So, you are very likely to hear or read something like this:
The population of Japan is aging quickly.
Dr. J: What else can we say about population? Two related nouns include overpopulation and underpopulation. 
JR: Overpopulation means too many people; underpopulation means too few people. 
Some countries once had an overpopulation problem, but with lower birth rates, now the problem is underpopulation.
DR. J: Both of these nouns are generally used in the noncount forms. In other words, we don’t generally make them plural. 
JR: And that’s Everyday Grammar.

title: Everyday Grammar Video: Talking About Mental Health
description:
JR: What’s new, Dr. Jill?
Dr. J:  Hi, John, I’ve been reading about mental health. There’s a study that says many people will have some mental health condition by age 75. 
JR: I’ve noticed that people are talking more openly about mental health these days.
Dr. J: Yes. Since the pandemic, schools have found ways to help children learn how to talk about mental health. And everyone can learn how to have good mental health. 
JR: Let’s look at the grammar: “mental health” has the adjective “mental” and the noun “health.” Together, they make a compound noun meaning the conditions around one’s mental and emotional well-being.
Dr. J: The word “mental” contrasts with the word “physical.” In the past there was a clear difference between mental and physical health. But these days we are learning that physical health can be closely tied with mental health. 
JR: We know the opposite of health is illness. So if there is something affecting someone’s mental health, you can say it is a mental illness. 
Dr. J: Examples of mental illnesses include depression and anxiety. Anxiety means feeling worried, tense, or nervous.
JR: When we talk about someone’s mental health, it is important to use the right words. We want to be respectful of the person and understanding of their situation. 
Dr. J: That’s a good point, John. We can use language that is centered on the person rather than their mental health issues.
JR: Can you give me an example, Dr. Jill?
Dr. J: One way to do this is to say a person is “living with” their condition.
The structure for this is: Subject + verb live + preposition with + noun form of illness.
Kurt lives with anxiety.
JR: We’ll talk more about that in our next lesson. 
Dr. J: And that’s Everyday Grammar!
Episode # 171 Talking Kindly About Mental Illness 
JR: In our last lesson, we talked about the best words and language to use when talking about mental health and mental illness.
Dr. J: We said that it’s best to use person-centered language. Here is one structure: 
Subject + verb live + preposition with + noun form of illness.
JR: An example is 
Bill lives with depression.
Dr. J: Another way you can talk about mental illness is to use this structure: 
Subject + verb have + noun form of illness.
JR: Using that form, we would say, 
Amy has anxiety.
Dr. J: It’s important to remember that we avoid using informal words like “crazy” to talk about a person with a mental illness. That kind of language can be harmful.
JR: Experts say using such words can lead to stigma. Stigma is a set of negative beliefs that a culture has about something. 
Dr. J: Stigma can prevent people from seeking help with their own mental illnesses. And before we go, I think we should talk about ways to have good mental health. 
JR: Good idea, Dr. Jill. I know for me, doing something creative like making music helps to keep me happy. 
Dr. J: And I enjoy my volunteer work – helping other people makes me feel good. 
JR: Some other ways are to exercise or learn breathing methods, or to just take a break from your routine.
Dr. J: Hey, that’s great advice. Let’s take a break now!
JR: And that’s Everyday Grammar!

title: Interactive Writing in Kindergarten:  Writing about Reading
description:
Interactive writing is a great component in balanced literacy where students receive a high level of support that enables them to look closely at letters, sounds, and words.  They are using everything they've learned in the foundational skills, to then make meaning of it, and compose a piece of writing together.  The students that helped compose the piece were strategically chosen based on their Words Their Way data.  It is very important to use the resources around the room such as; an alphabet chart, word wall, student name list, etc. where you are modeling good habits of making meaning with everything around you.   

Since we are at the end of the year, our interactive writing should also reflect the students' data at the end of the year.  I decided to focus on our shared reading book (found in Benchmark) discussing characters and character traits.  With prompting and support, I was able to guide the students to understand the actions portrayed by the characters  determined what kind of person they were.  

The students shown in the video have great stamina and were excited to 'interact' with the piece.

title: Writer's Workshop 1st Grade Editing Lesson
description: Since this is the beginning of the year, we want to make sure that students are held accountable for the sight words they learned from kindergarten.  We also want to make sure that students can read AND write the kinder sight words because the purpose is transferring the skills from one content to another.

title: Narrative Shared Writing Lesson- Kindergarten Writer's Workshop
description:
Shared writing is my favorite time of the day!  This is when the class is gathered together to recreate and retell something that happened in the class so everyone can participate and create a 'shared writing' together.  The students are practicing retelling a story with beginning, middle, and end and as the teacher, we are taking care of the drawing and writing for them.  

Since I needed a 'shared' experience with the kindergarteners, I told them to play "Ring Around the Rosie," with me and that would be our shared experience together.  The students were able to retell the experience and with more practice, it'll come more natural for them to retell with beginning, middle, and end.  

I can't emphasize enough how important the experience should be "together" so the students can help retell the story since they were part of it.  Not only does this help with oral rehearsal of a narrative story, but it will support the students in reading workshop as well.

title: All About Shared Writing- Informational Unit Kindergarten
description:
This shared writing lesson is one component of balanced literacy and is introduced either during the immersion phase of a new writing unit, or can be continued while working in the unit of study for extra practice and support.  

The purpose of shared writing is to demonstrate the writing process where the teacher HOLDS the marker and the students are sharing their ideas to help compose the text together.  The shared writing book can also be used during your writing workshop mini lesson as part of your active engagement so students can practice with a piece they're familiar with before starting on their own piece.  

The part of the writing process I'm demonstrating during my shared writing lesson, is how students think about a topic they know "all about," sketch across the pages to hold onto each page, and touch and tell across the pages.

title: Shared Reading Day 2
description: This shared reading video shows the second day in Ms. Manor's 1st grade classroom. The focus of the lesson was phonics and phonemic awareness. The students did a great job using their white boards and sound spelling cards to think about words that have the same spelling patterns as the ones listed in the book.  It is very important to emphasize to students that if they know how to read and write one word, they can read and write multiple words that have the same spelling patterns- so when they're reading independently and get to a "tricky" word, they have one way of trying to figure out the word.

We have to remember, it's all about students' transferring what they're learning in phonics to their reading and writing so we have to make that connection explicit for them.  It's great that the word wall was easily accessible for the teacher and students because the more we reference the word wall the more the students will refer to it as well! And... that's the whole point of having one in your classroom!  Transfer, transfer, transfer!

title: Shared Writing for Small Moments
description:
This shared writing lesson is one component of balanced literacy and is introduced to Ms. Marrufo's 1st Grade class during her immersion week OR anytime there's an opportunity to create a shared "experience" together.  Her students are working on personal narratives (small moments) and I created an "experience" together by dropping my markers- which led to a narrative we could ALL participate in and create our shared writing together!

The purpose of shared writing is to demonstrate the writing process where the teacher holds the marker and the students are sharing their ideas to help compose the text together.  Shared writing is also used as a preview of the new writing unit that the students will be starting independently the following week.  The lesson takes about 8-10 minutes and everyday the teacher will continue to compose the piece with the students by practicing:  
-touching and telling the story across the pages 
-working on adding details to the illustrations
-labeling
-writing
-rereading the piece for clarity

title: Shared Reading Day 3
description: This shared reading video shows the third day in Ms. Manor's 1st grade classroom. The focus for day 3 was working on word work and covering certain words with post-its. These words were selected because I felt there was enough support in the illustrations to guide the students at choosing the correct words that were covered. Certain words were covered such as, "sighed" and "groaned" because I knew the students wouldn't have anticipated that word without doing meaning work by looking at the pictures first and thinking which spelling patterns matched the word that was covered.  As they were guessing, I would uncover the first letter to see if that matched the meaning work the students were doing first. When studying the three cuing systems, most of the students guessed "said" and "growled" which made sense (meaning work) and sounded right (syntax) BUT didn't look right (visual), so they had to really look throughout the entire word to see what would look right in the middle and end of the word.  The students did a great job pushing themselves to use their knowledge of spelling patterns.

title: Guided Reading Lesson 2nd Grade
description:
This guided reading lesson was taken with 2nd grade students working instructionally in level L and reading independently in Level K.  

When introducing a brand new series, I try to give students as much background knowledge on the characters they'll encounter.  I also try to show students what 'real' readers do when they pick up a book by checking to see if there's a blurb in the back that tells me a little bit of the story.  

As students are reading, I checked in with them individually to ask, "What's happening so far..." to monitor their comprehension (since that was the focus with this group).  

My teaching at the end of the lesson was one way that readers can use post-it's is to track the characters in their book because we want to make sure we know who the characters are.  The Continuum of Literacy Learning by Fountas and Pinnell is a great resource to learn about the new characteristics within the different levels and to familiarize yourself with the levels your students are tackling.  

This video also shows what the other students "could" be doing when you're working with a guided reading group.  This school has enough books to support students in a reading workshop model where students are reading a variety of books at their independent level.  IF your school does not have access to enough books, many other teachers use literacy centers, independent workshop time, or universal access time as a way where the teacher can work with one or two groups depending on the stamina of his/her class.

title: Guided Reading Lesson Kindergarten and First Grade
description: This guided reading lesson was taken with 1st grade students working independently in Level C. The book I chose was their instructional Level D and the genre was fiction. The title was called 'Sam and the Waves,' and I wanted to be as explicit as possible in my book introduction and ask the students about their experience with 'waves' at the beach instead of having them tell me 'all about the beach.' I also used the same sentence structure that is in the text "...they ran down to the beach" because the students would be encountering some high frequency words they weren't familiar with. As students were reading, I monitored and prompted as needed working on phonics, intonation, and fluency. After reading, I brought the group back together to focus on comprehension questions. I wanted the students to use the book to provide evidence to support their answers.

title: Kindergarten Shared Reading Day 3
description: This shared reading video shows a Day 3 in the same kindergarten class using the SAME narrative story called, "I Went Walking."  The focus of the lesson was phonics and phonemic awareness.  The students did an amazing job using their white boards and sound spelling cards to think about words that have the same spelling patterns as the ones listed in the book.  The students are able to bring their knowledge of the word study work they've been doing during word study time into the shared reading lesson.  Mrs. Hackman's class was amazing!!

title: 1st grade Interactive Read Aloud
description:
Interactive read aloud is the highest form of support that we can offer our students to hear how a proficient reader sounds while modeling places to stop and think aloud different skills we naturally do as readers.

If our students are lacking in retelling, do it some more during read aloud time.  If our students are lacking with inference skills, incorporate some more during read aloud time.  

We all know students are the most engaged when we read aloud to them- so incorporate many read alouds in many genres throughout the day- so they hear language all the time!

description:
Interactive writing in kindergarten is a great way to build a sense of community within your classroom while focusing on phonemic awareness and phonics skills.  This IS the best way to show how and why we learn sight words/high frequency words and how we transfer the words we are learning to our writing. title: Kindergarten and TK Small Group Interactive Writing Lesson
description:
Many people believe that interactive writing is primarily done in a whole group setting, but based on student data, (from running records and writing samples from writing workshop) the best small group instruction that demonstrates the early behavior characteristics of a Level A (according to Fountas and Pinnell) would be to create an interactive writing book together working with those students who need extra support moving from Emergent reading to a level A.  

The students that I'm working with, based on their running records, showed no evidence of one-to-one matching, showed no evidence of matching beginning sounds of words to the pictures shown, and showed no evidence of high frequency word knowledge.  

By creating a small book together, the students will take ownership of each page and also see how we use the high frequency words in context to make it more meaningful.    

The purpose of interactive writing is working on spelling practices, phonics, phonemic awareness, and writing conventions by "interactively" composing the piece together while sharing the pen.

title: Shared Reading Kindergarten
description:
Shared reading is a time in our day where we show students how print works with enlarged text, that are highly engaging and have wonderful illustrations and language that invite students in.  I have used these books multiple times by Brand New Readers and highly recommend purchasing them for shared and guided reading (levels A-D).  My focus is on letters and sounds, looking at word parts, and most of all using the illustrations to build meaning (comprehension work) which is always at the forefront.  The illustrations and story line in these books are funny and have "kid friendly" topics.  The illustrations lend themselves to have higher language support, which promotes vocabulary development and higher level thinking.  

I can reread this text with the students and create a shared or interactive writing based on the lesson/central message of the book, which I was asking the students at the end of the lesson, "What advice would you give the character?  Don't be afraid to try something new, because you might like it!  Give things a chance."  

I also wanted to try a different approach with my word work since I've analyzed the students' writing and know that some of them are ready to look at parts of words (word families) to solve a tricky word.

The energy that exudes from the kindergarteners is how shared reading should look and feel.

title: Kindergarten Shared Reading Day 2
description: This was the 2nd day in a kindergarten classroom demonstrating a Shared Reading lesson.  The focus for day 2 was working on word work and covering certain words with post-its.  These words were selected because I felt there was enough support in the illustrations to guide the students at choosing the correct words that were covered.  As they were guessing, I would uncover the first letter to see if that matched what was in the pictures.  The students did a phenomenal job in Mrs. Hackman's class which shows how much background knowledge and word work they've been doing throughout the year!  Great job Mrs. Hackman!!!!

title: Using a Mentor Text in Writer's Workshop- 1st grade and Kindergarten
description:
In this video, we will be studying how the author George McClements uses speech bubbles in his book Night of the Veggie Monster to make his characters talk and their stories come to life.  

This book is a great mentor text for reading and writing because there are so many opportunities to stop and have a discussion about the topic ALONG with adding a writing about reading piece afterwards OR creating an interactive opinion writing book using the students in your classroom..."Room ____'s Favorite Vegetables" or "Meet the Veggie Monsters in Room _____'s."

The mini-lesson was adapted from the 1st grade UOS Session 14.  This is my version of the lesson.  

Connection:  We just read Night of the Veggie Monster and George McClements did something special in his book that we can try in our own writing.  

Teaching Point:  So today I want to teach you that we can write just like George McClements by adding speech bubbles in our stories to make our characters come to life and then adding it to our words. 

Active Engagement:  Now it's your turn to try with your stories you brought to the carpet.  Find a place where you can write just like George McClements by adding a speech bubble where your characters are talking to make them come to life.  

Link:  Today and everyday, when you're writing and want to make your characters talk, you can add a speech bubble to make your characters come to life.  

I would start to create a chart with the different craft moves from George McClements so students have a place to refer to when they're writing independently.
